title: Not a 1 promt game but 3 months project to build something I can't code on my own, or afford a professional to team up.
author: 8WayPixels
selftext:
I'm not a programmer, and I'm not even a game designer. My experience is mostly in animation, and even then, I don't have the time to sit down and create the full mountain of assets a game needs because I have a full-time job.

Like many of you, I want to make a game. I've tried teaming up with people before, but at some point motivation tends to fade when there's no way to self-fund the project. I've also tried getting some code going for my own projects with LLMs in the past, but I always ended up hitting dead ends and limitations after barely scratching the surface of what a real game requires.

This time feels different.

I'm using Godot + Codex, and for the first time, things are actually getting pretty deep. It genuinely feels like I might be able to get somewhere with this.

I tend to fall into rabbit holes with ideas and mechanics that I previously couldn't even get close to implementing. On top of that, my experience with the actual production side of a videogame project — management, scope, file organization, all the sheer volume of stuff involved — is basically nonexistent. So I'm learning all of that by going through it for the first time.

And boy, is it deep. 😅

For this first attempt, I deliberately set a very narrow scope, thinking, "Oh, this should be easy because it looks simple." I decided to recreate the core mechanics of Shogun Showdown as closely as possible, while trying very hard not to let my own "magnificent" ideas derail the scope.

Of course, once things started taking shape, I couldn't help myself and added a couple of things of my own — two mechanics that I personally wanted to have: a defensive mechanic for spending a turn in place, and a replay system.

There's still a LONG way to go. A lot of placeholder art waiting for future sprite updates, plenty of broken or misplaced sprites, unfinished systems, questionable decisions... you name it.

But honestly, I'm just really happy that I've managed to get this far.

For someone coming into this with basically zero programming and game-development experience, seeing an actual game start to emerge from all those little pieces is pretty damn exciting.

Still learning, still breaking things, still fixing them — but for the first time, it really feels like I'm making a game. ❤️

replies.author: 8WayPixels
replies.body:
I get what you're saying, but I think you're misunderstanding what I'm trying to say.

I'm not claiming that prompting “build me something identical to X” is some incredibly difficult technical achievement. That's not the point of my post. I'm saying that, for someone with my background, actually managing the process and understanding everything that goes into making a game work and feel coherent is much bigger than I ever imagined.

I'm not doing this with one prompt and calling it a day. I'm following an actual workflow, iterating, debugging, making design decisions, breaking things, fixing them, and learning game design by being directly involved in the process. I'm not calling myself a game designer or a game developer — I'm just a guy with very little experience trying to figure out how to make something happen.

And yeah, I'm proud of it. Even if you think it's easy, that's okay. You clearly have more experience with this than I do, and I'm not trying to compete with that.

For someone with my profile — a full-time job, a couple of hours a day to work on this, no budget to hire a professional programmer, and basically no game-development experience — getting to this point is actually a pretty big deal.

And honestly, that's what I'm trying to share. Learning isn't showing off. I'm documenting the process because I think there are probably other people out there who have ideas they want to make real but don't have the skills or budget to do it the traditional way.

And yes, starting by recreating a system from a game you like is, in my opinion, a pretty damn good way to learn how that system actually works.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body:
Good job OP. And good job explaining yourself in this reply too.

Obviously samurai showdown is going to jump into everyone’s head watching the video. But it’s also got some cool elements. I like the realtime bar you added, it adds an interesting element to the gameplay. I am curious though, samurai showdown is great because you can see the enemy actions and basically plan out your sequence of attack and who dies after each action. Now does the realtime aspect actually reduce from that core gameplay fundamental concept by adding an element of probability and unpredictability? By adding this cool new thing are you weakening a core fundamental of the original game? Just curious if you e thought about that

Anyway great job, keep iterating and creating and polishing. Dad of 2 here with a full time job working on my own game so I know how hard the time constraints make it

replies.author: 8WayPixels
replies.body:
Hey, thank you very much for the feedback, and especially for the thoughtful question!

Yes, I deliberately made the decision to add a dynamic mechanic with a degree of human timing/skill, breaking away from the purely mathematical predictability of the original system.

I've always loved parry, deflect and evade mechanics in classic fighting games. There's something I absolutely love about successfully executing one at the right moment, so I wanted to bring a little bit of that feeling into this system.

So yes, this simple addition does break with a very well-established and carefully designed structure from the original game, and I know that's a risk, my intention is that it gives a "spent" turn in place a chance to change the course of a fight.

And thank you for understanding, good luck with your game too, dad of 2! :)

replies.author: 8WayPixels
replies.body:
I actually think this is an interesting moment for developers rather than the end of personal software development.

I'm coming at this from the opposite direction. I'm an animator/artist with basically no programming or game-development background, and AI tools are allowing me to get much further into something that I simply couldn't have attempted on my own before.

But I'm also discovering that getting something to run is very different from actually making something good. The deeper I get into the project, the more I realize how much knowledge goes into game design, architecture, scope management, debugging, UX, balancing, production, etc.

AI has lowered the barrier for me to *participate* in that process, but it hasn't removed the process itself.

And honestly, if you're a good software developer, I'd imagine these tools could make you even more productive rather than useless. There will probably be a lot more people making their own little games and software, but someone still has to understand what they're building when things get complicated.

I'm basically the guy on the other side of the fence who finally got a chance to climb over it. 😅

comments.author: Jolly-Rip5973
comments.body:
The animation looks pretty good the basic game play seems solid. That's something I might actually play.   
  
But man that's literally 1980s graphics. 

Reminds me of Commodore Amiga graphics. Honestly it's little worse than Amiga Graphics, maybe Atari 800 level or Early IBM PC.   
  
Maybe that's ok, but if you are going for nostalgia, going back that far, your average player would need to be mid to late 50s.  

It's pretty interesting to me that so many games even by A studios look worse than graphics for early 2010s. 

Batman: Arkham Asylum from 2009 looks better than many modern unreal engine games.   
  
I realize you're probably a one man dev team with no art training but i also imagine you could probably 4X the resolution and character pixel count, use a gen Ai model to create interesting 2D characters and then use Claude, Gemini or ChatGPT to extrapolate the animations.    
  
Those extrapolations would probably need some manual cleanup. There are pixel animation cleanup programs though.    
  
I would try to increase the resolution of the models and polish it up more like a stylized 2D fighter. Maybe the character detail for 1998 King of Fighters level characters.   
  
You wouldn't need all the fancy fighting animations  just larger character detail to try and make them interesting looking. 

You could also create a base character for generic enemies and then just alter outfit colors or slight change so every enemy doesn't look exactly the same. Have like 8 different basic fighter enemies with exact same animation but slightly different color or outfit details. 

https://preview.redd.it/kev2ovap7hth1.png?width=1215&format=png&auto=webp&s=917edc62647e4708f503a03445ecf29c853cb669

replies.author: 8WayPixels
replies.body:
Thank you for the feedback, sir! I really appreciate it.

I am actually aiming for a bit of that nostalgia, but the main reason for the low resolution is also practicality. My current plan is basically: *do what I can with the time I have.*

I'm making the sprites small enough that I can actually animate them by hand and keep moving forward, while treating a lot of the current art as an MVP/placeholder that can be improved later.

For now, keeping the assets relatively small lets me spend more of my limited time figuring out the game mechanics, systems, and overall structure instead of getting stuck producing high-detail art for every single thing.

If I ever get the game to a point where the core systems are solid, I'd love to revisit the art and push the characters much further. For now, I'm trying to make something I can actually finish rather than something that looks great but never gets completed. :)
